My verdict: **the second colleague is more right**. I would not call this “just paying other countries to take our problem” as the main explanation.

Climate change is a global physical problem: a tonne of CO₂ avoided abroad is as good as a tonne avoided in Switzerland. There is no “Swiss carbon” in the atmosphere that Switzerland owns and can hand over. If Swiss money can cause more verified, additional CO₂ reductions per franc abroad than it can domestically, then using part of the target for projects abroad can make the overall policy more effective.

The “paying others to take our problem” line is a useful warning, but it is the wrong frame unless the projects are fake, weak, or double-counted. The real question is: **does the Swiss payment cause a reduction that would not otherwise happen?** If yes, that is real global emissions reduction. If no, then it is just a credit and the first colleague is right in spirit.

So I side with the “cheapest way to cut real emissions” argument, with a strict definition of *real*: the project must be additional, not double-counted, and durable. Under that standard, the Swiss rule is not cheating; it is a capped way to buy cheaper global abatement while still requiring most cuts at home.
